concepts.name: Vectors, force representation, and lines of action
concepts.why_this_depth: Prerequisite foundation owned by Topic 1 (9702_t01); a force is a vector with magnitude, direction, point of application, and an extended straight line of action.
misconceptions: Confusing the length of a physical body with the line of action of an applied force.
Assuming a force acts only at a single point without having an extended collinear line of action.
demands: Recall that forces are vectors represented by directed line segments.
Recall that every force has an infinite imaginary line of action extending along its direction.

concepts.name: Mass, gravitational field strength, and weight calculation (W = mg)
concepts.why_this_depth: Prerequisite calculation owned by Topic 3 (9702_t03); weight is the downward gravitational force acting on a mass in a gravitational field.
misconceptions: Conflating mass in kilograms with weight in newtons.
Omitting multiplication by gravitational field strength g (9.81 N kg^-1 or m s^-2) when converting mass to weight.
demands: Recall and apply W = mg to calculate weight from mass.
Identify that weight acts vertically downward toward the centre of the Earth.

concepts.name: Centre of gravity and distributed weight replacement
concepts.why_this_depth: Directly carries owned outcome 9702_t04_m01_o01 and controlled definition 9702_def_centre_of_gravity; tested across P2 questions (9702_s17_21_q03_b_i, 9702_s22_21_q02_a, 9702_s19_22_q03_a, 9702_s23_22_q02_a).
misconceptions: Believing the centre of gravity is always at the geometric midpoint regardless of mass distribution.
Thinking weight acts throughout an object as multiple separate forces rather than being represented by a single equivalent downward vector.
Assuming the centre of gravity must lie inside the solid material of a body, ignoring ring or hollow geometries.
demands: State verbatim definition: the point through which the whole weight of a body may be considered to act.
Identify that for uniform symmetrical objects the centre of gravity lies at the geometric centre.
Deduce qualitatively that the centre of gravity shifts towards regions of greater mass concentration in non-uniform objects.
Represent distributed gravitational pulls by a single downward vector arrow W acting through the centre of gravity.

concepts.name: Pivot, line of action, and perpendicular distance (d_perp)
concepts.why_this_depth: Essential geometric prerequisite for moment definition and calculation in owned outcome 9702_t04_m01_o02.
misconceptions: Using the direct straight-line distance along a body rather than the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action.
Failing to extend the line of action forward or backward to construct the perpendicular distance.
Believing perpendicular distance is measured to the point of force application rather than to the line of action.
demands: Identify the pivot (point about which rotation or turning is considered).
Draw and extend the line of action of an applied force.
Construct and identify the shortest perpendicular distance (d_perp) from the pivot to that line of action.

concepts.name: Definition and formula of the moment of a force (M = F d_perp)
concepts.why_this_depth: Carries owned outcome 9702_t04_m01_o02, definition 9702_def_moment_of_force, and formula 9702_formula_moment; tested in 9702_s21_23_q03_a, 9702_w17_22_q02_a, 9702_w20_21_q01_a_i, 9702_s25_22_q02_a.
misconceptions: Defining moment as simply 'force times distance' without specifying perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action.
Dividing force by distance (N/m or N m^-1) instead of multiplying.
Using joules (J) as the unit of moment instead of newton metres (N m).
Believing an object must be actively rotating for a moment to exist.
demands: State verbatim definition: the product of the force and the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force.
State and apply M = F d_perp in calculations.
State the coherent SI unit as newton metre (N m) and deduce SI base units (kg m^2 s^-2).
State the sense of the moment as clockwise or anticlockwise about the pivot.

concepts.name: Zero moment for a force whose line of action passes through the pivot
concepts.why_this_depth: Directly tested in Cambridge explanation questions (e.g. 9702_s19_22_q03_b_ii) and essential for analyzing pivot forces without invoking full equilibrium.
misconceptions: Assuming that applying a large force always creates a turning effect, even when directed straight at the pivot.
Confusing distance along a rod with perpendicular distance to the line of action when the line passes through the pivot.
demands: Explain why a force whose line of action passes through the pivot produces zero moment (d_perp = 0, so M = 0 N m).
Identify forces in a diagram that exert no turning effect about a chosen reference point.

concepts.name: Calculating the moment of an object's own weight
concepts.why_this_depth: Synthesises owned outcomes 1 and 2 by combining W = mg with M = F d_perp; directly assessed in 9702_s21_23_q03_b_ii, 9702_s17_21_q03_b, 9702_s22_21_q02_b_i, 9702_s25_22_q02_b_i.
misconceptions: Using mass in kg directly in the moment equation without converting to weight in newtons.
Measuring perpendicular distance from the pivot to the end of the body instead of to its centre of gravity.
In non-uniform bodies, incorrectly placing weight at the geometric midpoint instead of at the specified centre of gravity.
demands: Calculate object weight using W = mg.
Apply weight vertically downward through the centre of gravity.
Determine the horizontal perpendicular distance from the pivot to the vertical line of action of weight.
Calculate the moment of weight about the pivot with correct magnitude, unit, and rotational sense.

concepts.name: Perpendicular distance geometry for angled forces and angled bodies
concepts.why_this_depth: Major discriminant in P2 examinations (9702_w17_22_q02_b_ii, 9702_w20_21_q01_c_i, 9702_s25_22_q02_b_i); students must evaluate trigonometric geometry accurately.
misconceptions: Multiplying force by the slanted length along an inclined object rather than finding the perpendicular distance.
Inverting sine and cosine when resolving angles measured from the horizontal versus the vertical.
Failing to recognize that because weight is vertical, the perpendicular distance from a pivot to its line of action is strictly the horizontal separation.
demands: Determine d_perp using right-angled trigonometry (d cos theta or d sin theta depending on angle definition).
Demonstrate the equivalence between F x d_perp and (F_perp) x d.
Calculate moments of angled forces or inclined bodies to appropriate significant figures.

concepts.name: Algebraic rearrangement of the moment formula to find force or perpendicular distance
concepts.why_this_depth: Required for multi-step calculation patterns where moment and one parameter are known, solving for required force F = M / d_perp or distance d_perp = M / F (e.g. 9702_s21_23_q03_b_iii).
misconceptions: Inverting the algebraic division when solving for distance (computing F / M instead of M / F).
Losing track of unit cancellation during algebraic rearrangement.
demands: Rearrange M = F d_perp algebraically to solve for F = M / d_perp or d_perp = M / F.
Substitute numerical values with units and verify dimensional consistency.

hook.historical_investigation: Archimedes of Syracuse (c. 287 - 212 BC) and his mathematical investigation of centres of gravity and the law of the lever in On the Equilibrium of Planes (c. 250 BC).
hook.why_this_spine: Archimedes established the foundational physical principle that an extended body with mass distributed throughout its volume can be mathematically replaced by a single point, its centre of gravity, through which the entire weight acts. He proved that the turning effect of an extended body depends strictly on the product of its weight and the perpendicular distance from the pivot, solving the puzzle of how asymmetric, non-uniform bodies balance.

verified_facts.fact: In circa 250 BC in Syracuse, Sicily, Greek mathematician and engineer Archimedes of Syracuse (c. 287 - 212 BC) composed his foundational treatise On the Equilibrium of Planes (Peri epipedon isorropion), establishing statics and the mathematical theory of the centre of gravity.
verified_facts.source: Heath, T. L. (1897), The Works of Archimedes, Cambridge University Press; Boyer, C. B. (1991), A History of Mathematics.

verified_facts.fact: Archimedes investigated how extended physical bodies balance when supported on a fulcrum, recognizing that before the turning effect of an extended object can be calculated, one must resolve how gravity acts on all its separate parts simultaneously.
verified_facts.source: Dijksterhuis, E. J. (1987), Archimedes, Princeton University Press, Chapter IV: The Elements of Statics.

verified_facts.fact: Archimedes introduced the rigorous postulate of the centre of gravity: the centre of gravity of any body is a definite point such that, if the body is suspended from that point, it remains at rest in whatever position it is placed, because the weights of its parts on either side of any line passing through the point balance each other.
verified_facts.source: Heath, T. L. (1897), The Works of Archimedes, On the Equilibrium of Planes, Book I.

verified_facts.fact: In Book I, Propositions 6 and 7, Archimedes proved the law of the lever: two magnitudes balance at distances reciprocally proportional to their weights, demonstrating that the distributed weight of an extended body can be treated as acting entirely at its centre of gravity.
verified_facts.source: Clagett, M. (1959), The Science of Mechanics in the Middle Ages, University of Wisconsin Press.

verified_facts.fact: In Book I, Propositions 9 to 15, Archimedes geometrically located the centres of gravity for parallelograms, triangles, and trapeziums, demonstrating that for symmetrical uniform shapes the centre of gravity lies at the geometric centre, whereas for asymmetric figures it shifts towards the region containing greater area and mass.
verified_facts.source: Heath, T. L. (1897), The Works of Archimedes, On the Equilibrium of Planes, Book I, Propositions 9-15.

hook.closing_question: How can an extended body with weight distributed along its entire length be represented as a single force, and how do we calculate the exact turning tendency produced by that force about any chosen pivot?

activities.reasoning_step: Predicting the qualitative location of the centre of gravity in an asymmetric body by analysing its mass distribution relative to its geometric boundaries.
misconceptions_addressed: Assuming the centre of gravity must always be located at the geometric midpoint regardless of mass distribution.
Believing that centre of gravity cannot lie outside the solid material of a body.

activities.reasoning_step: Deducing the coherent SI unit and base units of moment from its defining physical product, distinguishing it from energy and force-per-unit-length.
misconceptions_addressed: Confusing the unit of moment (N m) with division (N/m or N m^-1).
Treating newton metres as interchangeable with joules for turning effects.
Believing an object must undergo angular displacement for a moment to be non-zero.

activities.reasoning_step: Identifying which applied force vectors exert zero moment about a specified pivot by extending lines of action to determine zero perpendicular distance.
misconceptions_addressed: Believing any force applied to a body produces a moment even if directed through the pivot.
Confusing the length of the lever with the perpendicular distance to the line of action.

activities.reasoning_step: Synthesising weight calculation (W = mg) with centre-of-gravity placement to determine the magnitude and direction of the turning effect of an object's own mass about a pivot.
misconceptions_addressed: Using mass in kg directly in the moment equation without multiplying by gravitational field strength g.
Measuring the distance from the pivot to the edge or tip of the beam instead of to its centre of gravity.
Inverting the clockwise versus anticlockwise rotational sense.

activities.reasoning_step: Discriminating the true perpendicular moment arm from inclined physical dimensions using trigonometric resolution in angled force and body geometries.
misconceptions_addressed: Using the slant length of the inclined member rather than the horizontal perpendicular distance to the vertical weight vector.
Confusing sine and cosine when resolving angles relative to the vertical versus horizontal.
Failing to realise that the shortest distance from a pivot to a vertical line is strictly horizontal.

activities.reasoning_step: Rearranging the moment formula algebraically to determine required force or distance parameters while tracking dimensional consistency and unit cancellation.
misconceptions_addressed: Inverting the division when solving for distance (computing F / M instead of M / F).
Omitting unit cancellation during algebraic substitution.
